planting.note: Plant divisions or small starts in spring into very well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun; hardy yellow ice plant is more cold tolerant and slightly more shade tolerant than purple-flowered Delosperma cooperi, but still needs sharp winter drainage.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun; hardy yellow ice plant forms a dense, fast-spreading mat of small, glistening, bead-like succulent leaves that take on bronze-red tones in cold weather, studded in late spring with masses of bright golden-yellow, daisy-like flowers that open fully only in sunshine. It is among the most cold-hardy of the South African ice plants commonly grown in North American gardens, tolerating winter cold well beyond what its succulent appearance suggests, provided drainage stays sharp and the crown does not sit in standing winter moisture. Extremely drought tolerant once established, it thrives in rock gardens, dry slopes, and gravel mulch plantings where competition from other groundcovers is minimal. Shear back lightly after bloom if the mat becomes patchy or woody in the center, and avoid rich or poorly drained soil, which shortens its life considerably.

planting.note: Plant offsets in spring into very well-drained, gritty, lean soil in full sun to partial shade; like Sempervivum, the individual rosette flowers once and dies after producing a cone-shaped bloom spike, but offset rosettes continue the colony.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty, lean soil in full sun to partial shade; Chinese dunce cap forms tight, powdery blue-gray rosettes of fleshy, pointed leaves that closely resemble hens-and-chicks, spreading steadily by short runners that produce new offset rosettes around the mother plant. Its common name comes from the unusual conical flower spike that rises from a mature rosette in late summer to fall, densely packed with small white to pale pink star-shaped flowers, after which that individual rosette dies back, much like the related Sempervivum. Because offsets continually replace spent rosettes, the overall clump persists and slowly expands for years despite the monocarpic habit of any single rosette. It is easy to grow in rock gardens, trough plantings, and shallow containers, tolerating more shade than most true sedums while still requiring the sharp drainage typical of the succulent family.

planting.note: Plant small cuttings or divisions at any point in the growing season into very well-drained, dry, average to lean, neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Kamschatka stonecrop is one of the most widely used low sedum groundcovers in temperate gardens.

directions: Plant cuttings or divisions in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun to partial shade; Kamschatka stonecrop forms a dense, slowly spreading mound of toothed, spoon-shaped, glossy green leaves that flush attractive orange-red tones in fall and cold weather. Flat clusters of bright golden-yellow, star-shaped flowers cover the mat in early to midsummer, drawing bees and other pollinators, and the variegated cultivar 'Variegatum,' with creamy white leaf margins tinged pink, is nearly as widely planted as the plain green species. It tolerates more shade and slightly more moisture than many other low sedums, making it a versatile choice for rock gardens, border edges, and green roof plantings across a wide range of climates. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring if the center becomes bare or woody.

planting.note: Plant stem fragments or divisions at any point in the growing season into well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; stringy stonecrop spreads unusually fast for a sedum via long, thin, wiry runners that root at every leaf node.

directions: Plant stem fragments in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; stringy stonecrop is a fast, low, trailing sedum with whorls of narrow, bright yellow-green, succulent leaves along thin, wiry stems that root readily wherever they touch soil, spreading noticeably quicker than most other low-growing sedums. Clusters of small, star-shaped yellow flowers appear in early summer above the foliage, though the plant is grown chiefly for its rapid, dense groundcover habit rather than for floral display. It handles more shade and slightly more moisture than typical rock-garden sedums, making it useful for covering bare ground quickly under high, open shade or in a semi-shaded rock wall where faster establishment is wanted. Because it spreads so readily, confine it with a mowed edge, walkway, or container rather than placing it directly among smaller, choice rock garden plants it could overrun.

planting.note: Plant small cuttings or divisions at any point in the growing season into very well-drained, dry, lean, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; six-sided stonecrop is often confused with biting stonecrop but lacks its sharp, burning taste.

directions: Plant cuttings or divisions in very well-drained, lean, dry soil in full sun to partial shade; tasteless stonecrop forms a dense, low mat of tiny, cylindrical, bright green leaves arranged in neat, tightly spiraled rows around each stem, giving the foliage a distinctly geometric, six-sided appearance up close. Clusters of small, star-shaped yellow flowers cover the mat in early summer, similar to the closely related biting stonecrop but without the sharp, burning taste that gives that species its common name and mild toxicity warning. It spreads readily by rooting stem fragments to form a tough, walkable groundcover useful for green roofs, gravel gardens, and rock wall crevices where little else survives. Established mats need essentially no care beyond an occasional shearing if growth becomes woody or thin in the center, and they tolerate drought, poor soil, and heat with ease.
